summary.text: An otherwise-healthy 6-year-old female was admitted to hospital with diminished and then sudden loss of vision in the left eye, with moderate pain and monochromatic vision, over 12 hours before admission. Chickenpox exanthema had emerged six days before the ocular symptoms and she was highly febrile for the first few days. Her sister had been COVID-19 positive two months earlier; she had no COVID-19 symptoms, vaccination or tick exposure history.

Examination showed light perception in the left eye with a relative afferent pupillary defect, retinal whitening, a cherry-red spot and arteriolar attenuation without distinguishable emboli. OCTA and OCT showed left-eye capillary plexus disruption with decreased perfusion and retinal layer changes. MR angiography did not visualize the ophthalmic artery. Admission tests showed elevated D-dimers, IgM anticardiolipin and IgG anti-beta-2 glycoprotein 1 antibodies; CSF showed some pleocytosis with negative cultures, and echocardiography was normal. Left central retinal artery occlusion was diagnosed.

Immunology and infectious disease specialists were consulted for suspected antiphospholipid syndrome and chickenpox. She received intravenous acyclovir, methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisone, ceftriaxone, vitamin D and gastroprotection. Thrombolysis was not given because of late presentation, and enoxaparin was started. Fluorescein angiography four days after admission showed reduced capillary perfusion, delayed filling and leakage.

She recovered from chickenpox without non-ocular complications. IgM anticardiolipin became weakly positive at 29.7 CU one month after admission. Left eye blindness persisted without improvement, with marked retinal nerve fiber layer reduction on OCT at 3 and 5 months. No underlying systemic cause was found; varicella vasculopathy was considered possible.

evidence.quote: The symptoms emerged over 12 h before the admission
Considering that the symptoms started over six hours earlier than the admission

ambiguities.issue: The onset interval is given as over 12 h before admission (and vision loss lasting over twelve hours in the abstract) and as over six hours earlier than admission in the thrombolysis sentence. Both are lower bounds and over 12 h satisfies over six hours, so this is not a source conflict; no single onset time is stated.
ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not infer an exact onset time or a thrombolysis eligibility window.

ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not infer the date of the fever relative to the exanthema or ocular symptoms.

article_limitations: Figure pixels are described only in visual.json; the annotation figure rows stay caption-level.
Table 2 has no time column; only IgM aCL and IgG aβ2GP1 carry admission timing from the abstract sentence.
CRP reference-range unit (g/L) differs from the value unit (mg/L) in Table 1 and is kept literal.
Enoxaparin dose unit printed as mg/dan is kept literal.
Discussion statements about literature, cited cases and general mechanisms are treated as background, not patient facts.
OCT and fluorescein angiography laterality comes from the Figure 2 and Figure 3 caption lead sentences that scope the listed findings; the narrative sentences name no eye.
